clinicalPearls: Strychnine causes generalised muscle rigidity and violent, exaggerated startle-provoked spasms with a fully preserved level of consciousness between episodes
Classic signs include opisthotonos, risus sardonicus and trismus, closely mimicking tetanus but with much more rapid onset after ingestion
Spasms are triggered by minimal sensory stimulation, so a dark, quiet environment with minimal handling is an important supportive measure
Unlike a true seizure there is no post-ictal confusion, because the mechanism is spinal disinhibition rather than cortical discharge
Severe sustained contractions can cause hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, lactic acidosis and myoglobinuric renal injury
Death results from respiratory failure due to spasm of the muscles of respiration and diaphragm rather than direct central depression
Management is supportive: aggressive control of spasms with sedation and neuromuscular blockade with ventilation when needed, plus treatment of hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis
Sources include some rodenticides and adulterated illicit drugs, and diagnosis is largely clinical with confirmatory analytical testing
reference.pathophysiology: Strychnine competitively antagonises glycine, the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter at postsynaptic receptors of spinal cord and brainstem motor neurons. Loss of this inhibitory tone removes the normal reciprocal control of motor neurons, so both agonist and antagonist muscle groups contract simultaneously in response to any stimulus. The result is generalised rigidity with intermittent violent extensor spasms while consciousness is spared, because the toxin acts on the spinal cord rather than the cortex. Sustained muscular hyperactivity generates heat, acid and muscle breakdown, and respiratory muscle involvement causes fatal hypoventilation.
additionalDifferentials: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Creatine kinase and myoglobin to assess rhabdomyolysis
Arterial blood gas and lactate for acidosis and ventilation
Renal function and electrolytes including potassium and calcium
Analytical confirmation of strychnine in blood, urine or gastric contents
redFlags: Frequent or prolonged spasms involving respiratory muscles
Marked rhabdomyolysis or myoglobinuric renal injury
Inability to maintain the airway or adequate ventilation
reference.prognosis: If ventilation and spasms are controlled early and complications such as hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis are managed, recovery within a few days is usual as the toxin is metabolised; untreated severe poisoning is rapidly fatal from respiratory failure.
pitfalls: Mistaking spasms for epileptic seizures and overlooking preserved consciousness
Excessive stimulation, examination or lighting that provokes further spasms
Failing to secure the airway and provide ventilation once neuromuscular blockade is used
Delaying sedation while awaiting analytical confirmation
